video_title: Midterm Blood Bath, $4T AI Sell Off, Data Center Freeze, What’s Next for Trump
gist: After a Democratic midterm sweep (both chambers, 29+ governorships, Texas flipping), the besties debate whether the Iran war and its gas/diesel-driven inflation (2.4% to 3.7%, a rate hike, ~7.5% mortgages) or a structurally broken wage-earner economy caused it. The bigger market story is a ~$4T AI sell-off on fears that new governors freeze data center permits, which Chamath argues makes hyperscalers kingmakers over compute-renting neoclouds and frontier labs, with the SpaceX-Anthropic 90-day out as the key trigger; Sacks expects 2027 capex to hold but the 2028 pipeline to shrink sharply.

themes.theme: Midterm postmortem: war-driven inflation vs. broken economy

insights.claim: Democrats swept both chambers in the 2026 midterms, winning at least 29 governor races, 54-56 Senate seats and at least 250 House seats, while flipping deep-red states including Texas, Kansas, Iowa and South Carolina that Trump won by double digits in 2024.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A Watergate-scale repudiation sets up divided government and state-level power shifts that directly hit AI infrastructure policy.
insights.quote: Dems will have at least 250 seats, maybe even 260.

insights.claim: Sacks attributes the Republican loss to the Iran war and its economic consequences: gas went from about $3 to over $4, diesel higher, feeding food, freight and fertilizer costs and lifting inflation from 2.4% in January to 3.7%.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Energy-price shocks transmit quickly into broad inflation and political outcomes; oil is the key macro variable to watch.
insights.quote: Well, you got inflation going from 2.4 to 3.7%. again mostly driven by the cost of gas and diesel

insights.claim: Instead of the multiple 2026 rate cuts the market expected in January, the Fed delivered a rate hike that pushed mortgage rates to roughly 7.5%, feeding the affordability narrative.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Rate path reversed from easing to tightening, a headwind for housing and rate-sensitive assets until oil falls.
insights.quote: You end up getting a rate hike that brought the cost of mortgages to roughly 7 12%.

insights.claim: Sacks says underlying macro remains solid: a robust jobs report with upward revisions, unemployment near a record-low 4.1%, first-half GDP growth of about 2.1-2.5% and Q3 GDPNow tracking at 3.7%.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Real economy strength vs. perceived affordability gap means sentiment, not growth, is the binding political constraint.
insights.quote: You've got unemployment tick down to almost record low 4.1%.

insights.claim: Real post-tax household income rose about 3.1% in Trump's first year, but inflation outpacing wages over the last six months has started eroding those purchasing-power gains, and the average household now pays about $200 more a month on gas.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Consumer real income is rolling over, a risk to discretionary spending while energy prices stay elevated.
insights.quote: the average household is paying 200 bucks a month more in gas cost.

insights.claim: Sacks shows prediction markets gave Republicans a large, stable Senate lead through 2025 (Liberation Day tariffs barely registered), and the shift began only in March 2026 after the Iran war started on February 28, 2026.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Prediction-market time series can isolate which shocks truly move political outcomes.
insights.quote: When did the war begin? February 28th of 2026. Very clear.

insights.claim: In exit polling, 74% of voters said the Iran war was crucial (34%) or a major factor (40%) in their Congressional vote, and young males swung 36 points against Republicans relative to 2024.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: The war fractured the GOP coalition, especially the podcast-driven young male cohort.
insights.quote: Young males flipped their vote by 36 points in this midterm relative to the 2024 election.

insights.claim: Sacks argues the war fractured the Republican base by alienating alternative-media figures such as Tucker Carlson, Joe Rogan, Theo Von and Megyn Kelly, on whom Republicans depend because legacy media is hostile.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Alternative media is now a swing distribution channel in US politics.
insights.quote: We lost all the podcast bros.

insights.claim: Chamath argues ideology no longer matters: a central swing bloc voting on economics gave Biden, then Trump, then the 2026 Democrats huge wins, signaling that the economy has decoupled from reality for wage earners while asset owners win in every rate and policy regime.
insights.speaker: Chamath Palihapitiya
insights.so_what: Expect violent electoral swings against any incumbent until wage earners feel ownership of the economy, raising policy volatility.
insights.quote: I do not think Democrats or Republicans matter.

insights.claim: Chamath cites as evidence that ideology failed: heavy campaign spending (e.g., Texas and Ohio Senate races) was wasted, and of 15 Republican seats redrawn via redistricting to capture them, Democrats won 11 and Republicans only one.
insights.speaker: Chamath Palihapitiya
insights.so_what: Money and maps lost their predictive power; economic messaging dominated.
insights.quote: Of the 15 Republican seats that were redrawn so that they could capture all of them, Democrats won 11 of them. Republicans only won one.

insights.claim: Chamath predicts an economic-populist platform will win the 2028 presidency for whichever party adopts it, and updates his priors away from top-down economics toward closing loopholes, ending federal loan underwriting, cancelling student debt and zeroing federal taxes below roughly $125-150k.
insights.speaker: Chamath Palihapitiya
insights.so_what: Populist tax and credit policy is likely on the table regardless of party; trickle-down assumptions are politically dead.
insights.quote: the economic populist platform will be the one that you can take to the presidency in 28.

insights.claim: Friedberg argues government spending is the fundamental driver of cost of living; ending DOGE (Elon left June 5, 2025) and keeping a ~$7T budget with a ~$2T annual deficit guaranteed rising costs and a drift to socialist-style policies.
insights.speaker: David Friedberg
insights.so_what: Persistent $2T deficits keep inflation sticky; watch the bond market as the referee.
insights.quote: The more the government spends the more expensive things get.

insights.claim: Friedberg says COVID-era doubling of government spending inflated everything including assets, benefiting asset owners while wage earners lost ground on healthcare, education, housing, food and gas.
insights.speaker: David Friedberg
insights.so_what: Fiscal expansion is the mechanism behind the K-shaped economy and the political backlash against it.
insights.quote: COVID was an accelerating moment for this unaffordability problem for people that don't own assets in the US.

insights.claim: Friedberg expects 2027 budget gridlock between the new Congress and the president, with $2T deficits continuing and the bond market signaling where costs are headed.
insights.speaker: David Friedberg
insights.so_what: Fiscal gridlock plus deficits is a term-premium risk for Treasuries.

insights.claim: Jason argues the polls and prediction markets were correct all cycle; per Nate Silver's Silver Bulletin, Trump's net approval fell from about +5% to -28%, driven sequentially by chaotic Liberation Day tariffs, summer 2025 ICE enforcement, Epstein files and then the war.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Prediction markets and quality polling deserve more weight than partisan narratives; Polymarket reportedly called ~99% of races.
insights.quote: Trump started the term at 5% plus net approval rating. He ended it at -28.

insights.claim: Sacks shows Trump's net approval rating maps closely to the price of gasoline.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Gas price is a tradeable proxy for political risk.
insights.quote: Trump net approval maps to the price of gas.

insights.claim: A Gallup study shows 93% of Chinese citizens think AI will mostly help people, versus 36% of Americans, placing the US fourth-to-last globally, below Afghanistan.
insights.speaker: David Friedberg
insights.so_what: US public hostility to AI makes the 'tech oligarch' narrative a potent political attack vector.
insights.quote: 93% of Chinese citizens think AI will mostly help people in the country.

themes.theme: Trump's last two years: path to redemption

insights.claim: Sacks says ending the Iran war is the top three fixes; Brent fell 10% on election day merely on war-ending odds, and he expects Brent (as high as $117) to drop from about $110 to $70 if the war ends, lowering gas, diesel and food prices and letting the Fed cut.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: A war-end is a large downside catalyst for oil and upside catalyst for rate-sensitive assets.
insights.quote: It'll go from 110 to 70 if this war ends.

insights.claim: Sacks predicts that if the war ends, Trump's approval could rebound to the 40s; if it continues, Republicans keep bleeding popularity.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Political recovery hinges on a single binary: war exit.
insights.quote: I think that Trump's popularity will rebound maybe back in the 40s.

insights.claim: Sacks frames the historical analogs: Clinton (1994) and Obama (2010) course-corrected after midterm routs and won re-election, while George W. Bush doubled down with the Iraq surge after 2006 and Republicans lost again in 2008; he warns neocons are pushing a similar escalation.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Escalation (strikes on targets like Kharg Island) would signal a 2006-2008 repeat for the GOP.
insights.quote: If you course correct and get out now, I think you'll have a very successful next two years.

insights.claim: Jason proposes Trump pre-emptively pardon his family and administration, then deal with Democrats on taxing margin loans against equity above $10M at 50% of the capital gains rate, a $15 minimum wage phased over four years, a ban on stock trading in office, healthcare and housing incentives.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Taxing buy-borrow-die margin loans is entering mainstream tech-investor discourse.
insights.quote: We should just say anything over 10 million, you tax it at 50% uh of the capital gains rate.

insights.claim: Chamath argues history may judge Trump like Reagan: closing the border and tariffs (if committed investment revives domestic manufacturing) will compound and look better over time, and Trump should trade economic concessions to Democrats for preserving the border.
insights.speaker: Chamath Palihapitiya
insights.so_what: Reshoring capex commitments are the long-dated test of the tariff policy.

themes.theme: $4T AI sell-off and the data center freeze

insights.claim: AI-linked stocks including Nvidia, SpaceX, Tesla, AMD and Micron sold off this week, wiping out close to $4 trillion in market cap in what Jason called the worst single day in stock market history by total dollars.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: The market is now pricing political risk to AI infrastructure buildout.
insights.quote: Close to $4 trillion in market cap wiped out.

insights.claim: Polymarket odds of an Anthropic IPO this year fell from 95% before the midterms to 71%, and the WSJ reported the IPO valuation could be about $1 trillion rather than the $1.5-2 trillion previously floated.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Frontier-lab IPO valuations are being marked down on compute-supply risk.
insights.quote: they're going to have a 71% chance of going public this year. It was 95% before the midterms.

insights.claim: Sacks warns Texas governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has said no new permits will be issued until new legislation passes; since under-construction data centers may still need late-stage permits (e.g., air pollution), this could strand half-finished projects.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Even 'under construction' capacity carries permit risk; markets may be too sanguine.
insights.quote: She simply says that there'll be no new permits issued until they pass legislation.

insights.claim: Sacks' base case is that fully permitted data centers get finished and capex stays meaningful in 2027, but by 2028 the pipeline will be closed or sharply reduced because no politician has an incentive to approve new projects after both parties ran attack ads against data center approvals.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: AI capex cliff risk in 2028 for semis, power and construction supply chains.
insights.quote: I would expect that the pipeline will either be closed or significantly reduced and that will have a big economic impact.

insights.claim: Sacks notes gigawatt-scale data centers cost around $50 billion and cannot be financed under conditions of regulatory uncertainty, injunction or community-strike risk.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Uncertainty alone, not outright bans, can halt new groundbreakings.
insights.quote: these gigawatt power data centers they cost around $50 billion.

insights.claim: Sacks argues public hatred of data centers is driven mainly by the perception they raise utility bills and use water while 'oligarchs' get rich and receive tax breaks, more than by AI job-loss fears.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Projects that credibly lower local power bills may be the only ones that get approved.
insights.quote: the big reason why people hate the data centers so much is they perceive that it's driving up their utility bills

insights.claim: At a Cochise County, Arizona hearing on a 6 GW SpaceX data center, SpaceX pitched 40% lower electricity costs, no water use and 20% lower property taxes, but the audience shouted them down, showing the issue is emotional rather than fact-based.
insights.speaker: Chamath Palihapitiya
insights.so_what: Local opposition is impervious to economic arguments, raising siting risk for all builders.
insights.quote: they're going to reduce electricity cost by 40%. They don't use water. They'll reduce property taxes by 20%.

insights.claim: Chamath expects incoming governors to end tax-break deals for megacap tech and demand directly measurable local economic impacts first, producing a data center slowdown.
insights.speaker: Chamath Palihapitiya
insights.so_what: Higher local cost of building compresses data center returns.
insights.quote: should it really be the case that the most powerful seven or eight companies need a tax break to invest 30,50 billion to then generate 345 $500 billion? Probably not.

insights.claim: Chamath argues a compute slowdown benefits hyperscalers (Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, Google, SpaceX) that own existing capacity, is very bad for neoclouds that rent, and is bad for compute-short frontier model labs.
insights.speaker: Chamath Palihapitiya
insights.so_what: Long capacity owners, short compute renters: hyperscalers become kingmakers.
insights.quote: I think it's very bad for the neoclouds because they're renters and it's pretty bad for the foundational models because they are so short this capacity

insights.claim: Chamath lays out hyperscaler game theory: keep renting (status quo), or divert incremental compute to their own models (e.g., Google to Gemini), which would degrade leaders' user experience and let Gemini catch up despite Anthropic and OpenAI's 60-90 day improvement loops.
insights.speaker: Chamath Palihapitiya
insights.so_what: Compute scarcity could reshuffle frontier model rankings in favor of vertically integrated players.
insights.quote: They're on a 60 to 90day loop in improving their models.

insights.claim: Chamath says the SpaceX-Anthropic compute deal has a mutual 90-day termination right; if SpaceX exercised it, it could reprice that compute at spot, likely 2-3x the current rate, forcing Anthropic to capitulate and signaling to all hyperscalers they are under-monetizing capacity.
insights.speaker: Chamath Palihapitiya
insights.so_what: SpaceX's Anthropic revenue could 2-3x; this single contract is the key tell for compute pricing.
insights.quote: SpaceX and Anthropic's compute deal has a mutual 90day out.

insights.claim: Chamath predicts that if spot compute spikes, neoclouds will be forced to spend all raised debt and equity buying whatever compute they can at any price, since the alternative is bankruptcy.
insights.speaker: Chamath Palihapitiya
insights.so_what: Neocloud balance sheets face a squeeze; watch for distress and consolidation.
insights.quote: the other path is assured destruction and bankruptcy for me because I am just out of the game.

insights.claim: Chamath argues that with constrained supply, existing long-term offtake contracts become negative-EV, and $/MW/month and GPU-hour prices will go 'through the roof', with capacity flowing to the largest balance sheets like Google and Meta.
insights.speaker: Chamath Palihapitiya
insights.so_what: Supply constraint is bullish for compute pricing and owners of energized capacity.
insights.quote: the dollar cost of a GPU hour is going to go through the roof

insights.claim: Google took over a Crusoe data center, which Chamath cites as hyperscalers co-opting the 'renter class' because they control the critical ingredient, power.
insights.speaker: Chamath Palihapitiya
insights.so_what: Power-rich neocloud sites are acquisition targets for hyperscalers.
insights.quote: Google just took over a Cruso data center

insights.claim: Jason pushes back that Elon's strong relationship with Anthropic and acrimony with Sam Altman make a compromise repricing more likely than throwing the capacity to spot.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Relationship dynamics may temper the most extreme compute repricing.

insights.claim: Jason predicts that if US governors restrict data centers, buildout shifts to Canada, Mexico, Singapore, Malaysia and, post-war, the Middle East, making the US a net importer of tokens; he calls offshore data centers and local desktop models the trend of the next two years.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Non-US data center geographies and edge/local inference hardware benefit from US permitting friction.
insights.quote: So offshore uh data centers will be the trend of the next two years.

insights.claim: Jason says his 20-person VC firm spends about $40-50k a year on AI subscriptions (mainly Grok and Claude) for an estimated ~$2M in value, with only 10-20% of corporate America using AI daily, implying 500-1,000x more compute demand as agentic use spreads.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Enterprise adoption runway supports long-run compute demand despite near-term supply politics.
insights.quote: So I think there's 500 to a,000 times the need for this.

insights.claim: Jason says he has been buying SpaceX and Tesla shares through the sell-off, calling SpaceX severely undervalued given its option to move data centers into space if terrestrial builds are blocked.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Space-based compute is framed as a hedge against terrestrial permitting risk.
insights.quote: SpaceX which is severely undervalued as a stock

insights.claim: Friedberg predicts government ends up regulating compute rather than chips or models, treating data centers like utilities to control who gets access to AI.
insights.speaker: David Friedberg
insights.so_what: Utility-style regulation would cap returns for data center owners.
insights.quote: I think the data centers end up being treated like utilities in the future

insights.claim: Friedberg argues calls to stop AI development are really bids for state control of AI, and puts the odds of far-left proposals to ban AI development, deployment or use well above 10%, citing hundreds of state laws and a California bill vetoed by Gavin Newsom.
insights.speaker: David Friedberg
insights.so_what: Patchwork state regulation is a growing compliance and deployment risk for AI companies.
insights.quote: So I actually think the calls to stop the development of AI are actually calls for them to have absolute control over AI

insights.claim: Sacks says it is 100% certain Democrats will push major AI legislation next Congress, likely a federal department of AI that must review and approve frontier models before release, which he frames as a censorship and surveillance regime.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Pre-release model approval would slow frontier-lab iteration and favor incumbents.
insights.quote: So, it's 100% that Democrats are going to make a major push for AI legislation in the next Congress.

insights.claim: Sacks expects a quid pro quo in which government gains power and the closed-model duopoly gains regulatory capture and moats.
insights.speaker: David Sacks
insights.so_what: Regulation could entrench leading closed labs at the expense of open source.
insights.quote: The government gets more power and the duopoly of closed model companies get more regulatory capture or moes around their business.

insights.claim: Chamath counters that any broad AI legislation will hit data centers and constrain supply so severely that real control accrues to Meta, Amazon, Google, Microsoft and SpaceX, leaving renting foundation model companies at risk.
insights.speaker: Chamath Palihapitiya
insights.so_what: Owners of power and compute, not model makers, capture the regulatory regime.
insights.quote: the renter class in data centers as of Tuesday is very much at risk

themes.theme: Science corner: OpenAI disproves exponential time hypothesis

insights.claim: Friedberg reports OpenAI published a 175-page paper showing 3-SAT can be solved in subexponential time, disproving the 1999 exponential time hypothesis, reportedly done end-to-end in under 10 days or even hours; third-party verification is still pending.
insights.speaker: David Friedberg
insights.so_what: Frontier AI is producing research-grade math breakthroughs, a tangible benefit narrative amid political backlash.
insights.quote: And what open AAI did is they disproved that. And they disproved it in a 175page paper.
